body: On 4 October 1965, the feast of St. Francis of Assisi, Paul VI landed in New York — the first pope to set foot in the Western Hemisphere, and the first ever to visit the United States. "Greetings to you, America," he said at the airport; "the first pope to set foot on your land blesses you with all his heart."

Greeted by Secretary-General U Thant, he addressed the General Assembly in French, in the organization's twentieth year. "No more war, war never again," he pleaded; "it is peace, peace, that has to guide the destiny of the nations of all mankind." The whole journey lasted fourteen hours and ended with Mass at Yankee Stadium.

In Rome the Second Vatican Council was then holding its fourth and last session; two months later, on 8 December 1965, the pope closed it. His one-day pilgrimage for peace set a pattern: his successors have returned to the same rostrum to speak for the Church before the family of nations.

body: When fire gutted the Romanesque cathedral of Chartres in 1194, the town's despair turned to hope when the relic of the Virgin's veil — brought from Aachen by Charles the Bald about 876 — was found unharmed. Kings, guilds, and peasants gave or dragged stone, and in little more than a generation the new church rose, the most perfectly Gothic of all cathedrals.

The consecration came in October 1260 — the 24th by the common reckoning, though some authorities give the 17th — and St. Louis is believed to have attended. The royal house had given richly: the upper windows were the gift of the king, of St. Ferdinand, and of the queen mother Blanche of Castile, who had died in 1252.

Her glass is her glory: the old count numbers near four thousand figures in her windows. Kings came to her as pilgrims — Henry III of France eighteen times, Charles V of France twice, and barefoot; and Henry IV, barred from Reims, was crowned at Chartres in 1594. The Revolution spared her, and two wars; she stands as she was consecrated.

body: Isabella I of Castile, born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, joined her crown to that of Ferdinand of Aragon and so laid the foundation of a united Spain. In 1492 the two sovereigns took Granada, the last Moorish kingdom, ending the long Reconquista, and in that same year sponsored the voyage of Christopher Columbus across the ocean.

A queen of fervent and practical piety, she promoted the reform of the Spanish Church and its religious orders, aided by Cardinal Cisneros. Yet her reign is remembered also for its shadows, told here without gloss: the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 and the expulsion of the Jews from her realms in 1492.

Worn by the deaths of her only son John and her daughter Isabella, she withdrew from the cares of government in September 1504. She died a little before noon on 26 November 1504 in the royal palace at Medina del Campo, and was buried, by her own wish, at Granada. A cause for her beatification was in time opened, and she is styled a Servant of God.

body: On 9 December 1905 the French Republic passed the law on the Separation of the Churches and the State, ending the Concordat of 1801 by which Napoleon and Pius VII had for more than a hundred years governed the relations of Church and State in France.

The state would no longer recognize or pay the Church, but only associations cultuelles — associations formed in each parish for the conduct of worship; failing such associations, the property of the churches was to be lost forever and handed over to the charitable establishments of the communes. Pope Pius X met the law with resistance: by the encyclical Vehementer Nos of 11 February 1906 he solemnly condemned it as unjust to God and destructive of the Church's rights.

By the encyclical Gravissimo Officii of 10 August 1906 the pope forbade the associations, fearing they would furnish the state a pretext for meddling in the Church's inner life and the laity a constant temptation to rule the parish; the state then treated the old church corporations as nonexistent and transferred their goods, excepting only the edifices still used for worship. The Church of France was stripped of its endowments, and the law of 1905, much amended, still frames French laïcité.

body: Of a Roman family that had already given the Church two pontiffs, Stephen III and Sergius II, Adrian was seventy-five when the clergy and people of Rome chose him, much against his will, to succeed Nicholas I. He had been married before taking orders, and his old age was saddened by a domestic tragedy.

He followed closely in the footsteps of his energetic predecessor. At Monte Cassino he readmitted the repentant King Lothair of Lorraine to communion only after exacting a public oath that he would take back his lawful wife Theutberga; and against Hincmar of Reims he upheld the unlimited right of bishops to appeal to the Sovereign Pontiff.

At the Eighth General Council, which he convened at Constantinople in 869 and guided through three legates, he effected the deposition of Photius and the restoration of unity between the East and the West. The Bulgarians he could not hold for the western patriarchate, but he seconded the saintly brothers Cyril and Methodius, and his endorsement of their Slavonic liturgy proved of enduring influence. He died on 14 December 872, exactly five years from his consecration.
